body: `should_block?` writes to the DB (it bumps match_count and last_match_at) but gets called from a validator. `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which validates again, so one signup attempt against a blocked address increments match_count by 2. Any other `valid?` call adds more. Validation shouldn't have side effects like this. Either record the match once, outside validation, or only count it when the save actually fails.

The lookup is an exact, case-sensitive string match (`where(email: email)`). `Bad@Spammers.org` or ` bad@spammers.org` gets past a block on `bad@spammers.org`. Normalize the email on both sides (strip + downcase, e.g. `Email.downcase`/`lower(email)`) when storing and when checking. Also note there's no escape hatch for plus-addressing or dot variants.

`match_count += 1` followed by `save` is a read-modify-write, so concurrent signups lose increments. The `save` also runs full validations, including a uniqueness query, and its return value is ignored. Use an atomic update instead, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`.

The domain regex isn't anchored at the end. With whitelist `example.com`, an address like `foo@example.com.evil.org` (or `foo@example.community`) matches and is allowed. With blacklist `mail.ru`, `foo@mail.rubbish.com` is wrongly blocked. This was carried over from User, but now that it's a reusable validator it's a good time to anchor it: `/@(#{domains})\z/i`. Also, only `.` is escaped, so any other regex metacharacters in the setting get interpreted.

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined on the class prototype. Every instance of this controller shares the same array, and it is never cleared. After an email is rejected once, it keeps showing as invalid for the rest of the page session, even if the server-side cause goes away (for example a uniqueness error on another field, or the admin unblocks the address). Initialize it in `init` (`this.set('rejectedEmails', Em.A())`) and consider resetting it when the modal opens.

The client pushes `result.values.email`, which is the server-side `user.email`, and then compares it to the raw `accountEmail` input. If the server normalizes the email (e.g. `new_from_params` or `Email.downcase` lowercases the domain), the two strings differ, `contains` never matches, and the field doesn't show the rejection. Push the email that was actually submitted, or compare normalized values.

`errors: user.errors.to_hash` exposes every validation message to the client. Together with the new `blocked` error, this lets anyone probe whether a given address is on the block list. The frontend treats any email error as "rejected", including uniqueness (`has already been taken`) and domain errors. That's probably fine, but make sure the key-based check (`result.errors.email`) still works: `to_hash` produces symbol keys, which serialize to the string `email`.
